notes.title: Olive trees and lampstands: Zechariah 4
notes.text: The image of two olive trees and lampstands echoes Zechariah's vision of a lampstand flanked by two olive trees, which the prophet identifies as the two "anointed ones" who stand by the Lord of the whole earth (Zech 4:2-3, 11-14). Revelation reuses the picture for the two witnesses. Who the witnesses represent is much debated (two individuals, the church, or the law and the prophets); the text itself does not settle it.
notes.source: Zechariah 4:2-14; see G. K. Beale, The Book of Revelation (NIGTC, 1999), on Rev 11:4

notes.title: Abyss, not a bottomless pit
notes.text: The Greek abyssos means the deep: in the Septuagint it renders Hebrew tehom, the ocean depths (Gen 1:2), and in Revelation it is the prison or realm of evil powers (Rev 9:1-2, 11; 20:1-3). "Bottomless pit" in the KJV is a literal reading of a-byssos (without bottom), but "abyss" better keeps the name of a place.
notes.source: Bauer-Danker-Arndt-Gingrich (BDAG), A Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament, s.v. abyssos

notes.title: Breath of life: Ezekiel 37
notes.text: The wording echoes Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones, where "breath" (Hebrew ruach, Greek pneuma in the Septuagint) enters the dead and they stand on their feet (Ezek 37:5, 10). Greek pneuma can mean breath, wind or spirit, so "the Spirit of life" (KJV) and "the breath of life" are both defensible; the Ezekiel echo is why KJV27 chose "breath", and the verse is flagged for review.
notes.source: BDAG, s.v. pneuma; Septuagint of Ezekiel 37:10
